metadata.file_name: 34. Miranda et al. (2021). Development of INSVAGRAM: An English Subject-Verb Agreement Mobile Learning Application.pdf
metadata.title: Development of INSVAGRAM: An English Subject-Verb Agreement Mobile Learning Application
metadata.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a small, purposively sampled group of fifth-grade students (n=132) and conducted interviews with five English teachers to identify the least mastered topic (subject-verb agreement). The manuscript does not describe the use of any ILSA-style complex survey design or sampling weights, and it does not report any weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures. Because the work is an application-development and needs-assessment study (questionnaire profiles and teacher interviews) rather than an achievement-score modeling study, there is no plausible PV/scaling framework requiring international weights. For replication, researchers should treat the results as descriptive of the sampled context unless a probability-based sampling design and corresponding weights are explicitly implemented and reported.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not analyze ILSA cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it develops a mobile learning application based on questionnaire profiles and teacher interviews. As a result, PV handling is not applicable because there are no PV-based achievement scores or PV benchmarks used as dependent variables. The manuscript also does not report any missing-data strategy for the questionnaire or interview data, which is a reporting gap for transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Purposive sampling was used because most fifth graders were at home and not allowed to go outside during lockdowns/quarantine in the Philippines. Respondents were selected via peers and social networks (teachers, parents, classmates). The analytic sample reported is 132 fifth-grade students aged 10–12; the paper does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond being fifth graders and being reachable through the described networks.

main_findings.dataset_used: ILSA literature synthesis (systematic review; no single student-level analytic micro-dataset)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ILSA literature synthesis (systematic review; no single student-level analytic micro-dataset) the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that The study develops INSVAGRAM, a mobile learning application targeting English subject-verb agreement, identified as the least mastered topic through interviews with five fifth-grade English teachers. It first surveyed 132 fifth-grade students (ages 10–12) using a content-validated Likert questionnaire to profile access to technology, technology aptitude, and preferred/available devices at home; results indicated frequent access to technology (M=4.33) and high technology aptitude (M=3.45), with smartphones as the dominant available and preferred device. Based on these needs-assessment findings, the application was designed for Android and structured into Learn and Play modes with 10 lessons, animated guidance, corrective feedback, and a progression mechanism requiring at least 50% correct activities in Play mode to unlock subsequent lessons. No machine learning model training, predictive evaluation, or achievement-score scaling is reported; therefore, there are no ML performance metrics or causal claims. The paper also notes that user acceptance testing (UAT) was not conducted due to ongoing lockdowns, limiting evidence about usability and learning effectiveness in real classroom or home settings. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.
